newsitem.title: USA: Mutual funds urged to improve risk disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Mutual funds urged to improve risk disclosure.

text.p: Risk disclosure by the mutual fund industry is inadequate and the industry should focus more on future risks, a group of economists said Wednesday.

"While investors know what happened to a fund's returns in the past, their primary need is to predict the likely range of a fund's returns in the future," the Financial Economists Roundtable, a group of mostly university economists including three Nobel laureates, said in a statement.
A fund's risk could be assessed based on how closely its return was linked to given indexes, the riskiness of each index and how closely the indexes moved together, the group said.

"The roundtable recommends that each fund manager provide a well defined index or portfolio of indexes so that investors can be informed of the fund's likely future exposures to major sectors of the security markets," the group said.
Funds should also subsequently report how their actual performance fared relative to the benchmarks, it said.
It said any chart of historical performances of the benchmarks should show their deviation from the average returns in the given period as well.
"Such a presentation emphasizes the effects of risk rather than historic average returns," it said.
"Both theory and empirical evidence indicate that history is a much better predictor of future risk than of future average return," it said.

Since predictions of future outcomes are subject to error, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission should provide a safe harbor by specific reference under SEC Rule 175 so that funds can provide honest best estimates without fear of later litigation, it noted.
The group's statement was based on discussions at its annual meeting in July, said George Kaufman of Loyola University of Chicago, a member of its steering committee.
